analysis.one_liner: Bars lenders from suing foreclosed homeowners for the leftover mortgage balance after a foreclosure sale.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2015 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never held a vote on it; it died when the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: When a home is foreclosed, the sale often does not cover the full mortgage. Today, in many states, the lender can go to court and get a "deficiency judgment" forcing the former homeowner to pay the shortfall out of other savings or wages. This bill would ban courts from issuing those judgments for federally related home mortgages taken out after the bill became law, while leaving any stricter state protections in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Families who lose their home to foreclosure would start over without a second debt hanging over them for the difference between the sale price and the loan balance.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits courts from entering a deficiency judgment — an order requiring the borrower to pay the balance left on the mortgage after a foreclosure sale — for federally related mortgage loans made after enactment [S2][S3].
It applies to federally related mortgage loans as defined under the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, which covers most home mortgages in the United States [S3].
It would not override any state law that is already more protective of homeowners, so states could keep stronger limits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and investors, who could no longer collect the unpaid balance after a foreclosure, and possibly future borrowers if lenders respond by charging more or lending more cautiously.

drawbacks.text: Lenders bear a real cost: after a foreclosure sale, any shortfall between the sale price and the loan balance would be absorbed by the lender rather than the borrower [S2][S3].

Lenders could respond to that risk by charging higher rates, requiring larger down payments, or tightening credit on new loans, shifting some of the cost to future homebuyers (general knowledge about how lenders price foreclosure losses; not addressed in the bill text).
The bill only applies to loans made after it became law, so homeowners already in trouble with existing mortgages would get no help [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a family that has already lost its home, being chased for tens of thousands of dollars more is a heavy blow, and stopping it would give a real fresh start. The cost falls on lenders, who price foreclosure losses across their portfolios, though some of that cost could reach future borrowers through rates and credit terms. The bill's biggest practical limit is scope: it would do nothing for people with loans already outstanding, who are precisely those at risk of foreclosure now.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Michelle Lujan Grisham of New Mexico introduced the bill on April 16, 2015 [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
On June 26, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, where it stayed [S5].
No further action was recorded through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and investors kept the right to pursue deficiency judgments against foreclosed homeowners, since the ban was never enacted. Homeowners at risk of foreclosure got no protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mortgage lenders, who kept collecting shortfall debts

for.name: Rep. Michelle Lujan Grisham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban deficiency judgments after foreclosure sales.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only cosponsor listed.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; the committee never reported the bill or scheduled a vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the Republican-led committee took no action, but no vote ever occurred to show a party split.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to collect the unpaid mortgage balance after a foreclosure sale, a debt currently recoverable in many states. That loss is the homeowner's gain: the same dollars are either paid by the foreclosed family or absorbed by the lender.

industries.industry: Investors in mortgage debt and mortgage-backed securities
industries.note: Deficiency collections are part of the expected recovery on home loans; eliminating them for new loans would slightly reduce recoveries on foreclosed properties.
